issue_context.title: [API Proposal]: Expand data validation attributes
comments: I couldn't figure out the best area label to add to this issue. If you have write-permissions please help me learn by adding exactly one [area label](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/docs/area-owners.md).
@geeknoid can you include the code samples that demonstrate where validation would happen?

I see, it looks like that calls back into the validation infrastructure in System.ComponentModel.Annotations - so this isn't proposing any new consumers/entry-points for this validation - just some new attributes that use the existing mechanisms.
Validation attributes are not something we plan to invest any time in going forward. It is unlikely we will accept any changes in this area.
@ajcvickers can you say more -- how did we end up with that perspective, was it resources, usefulness, or lack of adoption?
Also, can you say more about the cost of additions like these? What are the costs beyond the attribute itself (including the validation method)?

@danmoseley Attributes in `System.ComponentModel.Annotations` (aka "Data Annotations") are used in two ways:

1. As validation attributes, through inheritance of `ValidationAttribute`, which, if implemented correctly can be used by any code that understands validation attributes without that code needing to be updated to consume the new attributes.
2. As directives to consuming code as to the semantics of the annotated member. So, for example U.I. components may look for the `KeyAttribute` and choose to make input read-only, or look at `StringLength` and restrict the U.I. from allowing more characters than specified. This is independent of the attribute's use for validation and relies on the consuming code understanding the semantics of the attribute.

Use in validation has a few problems:

1. The validation for any given attribute can never be changed without it breaking any application that uses it. So, for example, the behavior for allowing empty strings with `Required` is problematic in many cases, but can never be changed. Similarly, the attributes don't do recursive validation, which people often want, but can't be added by default without breaking.
2. Validation is not performed in places where people expect it to be. For example, people expect `JObject` to be validated, but it never is, and we can never change that without breaking existing applications.
3. The localization story for validation messages is not great.

The problems are worse when the attributes are consumed directly:

1. Different consumers have different interpretations of what the attributes mean. This leads to a situation where `MaxLength` is applied to a property, and one consumer interprets this as number of bytes in the string, while another interprets it as number of characters. This leads to, sometimes subtle, behavioral differences in the consumers which means using an attribute for one thing can easily break code somewhere else.
2. Some consumers respect (in whatever way they think that should be) some attributes but not others. This is again very confusing, because users can't understand why an attribute is working on one place but not another, or assume it is working somewhere it is not.
4. After a new attribute is added, consumers must react to add support for it. Legacy code that uses these attributes will never react, and code still under active development may or may not react, further fragmenting the story for application developers. 

It would be great for .NET to have a modern validation system that does not suffer from these issues. However, that has never been high enough priority to be funded, and last time I checked nobody is really interested in taking on and owning such a thing, since experience has shown the existing system to be such as can of worms. Beyond that, it doesn't seem wise to further add to the current system, beyond maintaining behavior that already exists.
Btw, the only reason my team owns this area is because we added some new attributes for legacy EF over 10 years ago. We learned our lesson and never did that again! :-)
Thanks for writing all that up - I think it will be useful in future. @geeknoid I assume functionally everything works fine if you keep these attributes where you have them today.

I know the libraries folks are currently adding README.md to each library indicating the kinds of changes they take. This one could probably benefit from one. @jeffhandley could you maybe point @ajcvickers at an example in the recommended format?

@danmoseley Unfortunately, no this is somewhat of a deal-breaker for the project we're on.

As we want to move many of our components into the core libraries, these components depend on all these attributes. If the attributes don't make it to the core of the platform, then we would need to rewrite our components to not depend on the attributes, which would be a lot of busy work leading to likely lower quality experience of our customers.

@ajcvickers So if I'm reading your response correctly, you're basically saying that the current attribute-based validation model is broken in many ways, and you don't want to invest in expanding its feature set?

For our project, we have a lot of option types, and they are validated systematically using a code generator option validator, which leverages all the validation attributes in a reliable and predictable way. It has worked very well for us, and leads to high-quality state coming into our code, and high-quality errors being presented to the user.

> So if I'm reading your response correctly, you're basically saying that the current attribute-based validation model is broken in many ways, and you don't want to invest in expanding its feature set?

Yes.

> For our project, we have a lot of option types, and they are validated systematically using a code generator option validator, which leverages all the validation attributes in a reliable and predictable way. It has worked very well for us, and leads to high-quality state coming into our code, and high-quality errors being presented to the user.

That's great for a system used in a well-defined way by a private group of consumers. It's a different thing to add new attributes to the BCL where they will be available to all consumers of .NET who will have many different expectations and come up with many different ways of consuming the code. And especially since there is history around how this code should be consumed that goes beyond what you are doing.

> I know the libraries folks are currently adding README.md to each library indicating the kinds of changes they take. This one could probably benefit from one. @jeffhandley could you maybe point @ajcvickers at an example in the recommended format?

Yes, we've been adding them to lots of libraries the last couple weeks. The XML libraries is a good example: dotnet/runtime#77401

We have some updates on this that have been discussed via email--capturing them here too:

* We are going to invest in DataAnnotations during .NET 8
  * We are going to review these proposed attributes during the early stages of .NET 8
  * We will also reconsider past attribute proposals that have been punted or closed
  * There are some other DataAnnotations shortcomings and modernization opportunities we're discussing more, such as localization and possible source-generator based validation execution

Regarding these proposed attributes, I have some notes on the API shapes.

1. `Base64StringAttribute`
    * This would generally not be used for end-user UI scenarios, which makes it a bit unusual for DataAnnotations validator attributes
    * We should discuss if we want to be open to scenarios where the models being validated are not UI-oriented
    * There are plenty of other non-validation attributes in the namespace that are not UI-oriented
    * If we do open the door for those though, where will we draw the line? If we have a Base64String validator, would that inviteWellFormedJsonString or WellFormedXmlString?
2. `ExclusiveRangeAttribute`
    * This doesn't cover the scenario of only one of the minimum or maximum being exclusive
    * We should consider expanding `RangeAttribute` to enable the minimum and/or maximum to be exclusive
3. `LengthAttribute`
    * Other validation libraries I've implemented have supported attributes that are validator factories such that a single attribute can result in 0-N validators from being composed, even conditionally based on validation context
    * I've long wished we had taken that approach with DataAnnotations too, as `LengthAttribute` could literally just compose `MinLengthAttribute` and `MaxLengthAttribute`
    * Assuming we still don't pursue validator factories though, this seems like a reasonable attribute to add
    * We should consider adding `Exclusive` to `MinLengthAttribute` and `MaxLengthAttribute` too
4. `NonDefaultValueRequiredAttribute`
    * This should likely get special treatment like `RequiredAttribute` does, where it's validated in the first pass of validation before other value validators are invoked
    * `RequiredAttribute` already has `AllowEmptyStrings`; `AllowDefaultValue` (or something like it) could be considered as well
5. `RejectValuesAttribute`
    * This is essentially a "block list" validator; since block lists are often anti-patterns, I want to be cautious about this as a first-class validator
    * @geeknoid Can you elaborate on the scenarios for this one please?
    * I could imagine a different approach where we have something like `CompareValidator` but instead of comparing against another property, it compares against hard-coded value(s) with a comparison operator provided; we could also entertain expanding `CompareValidator` to allow the operator to be specified
6. `TimeSpanAttribute`
    * This can already be achieved with `[Range(typeof(TimeSpan), "<min-timespan-string>", "<max-timespan-string>")]`
    * If `RangeAttribute` offered properties for exclusive min/max, would that be sufficient?

With any changes to the existing attributes, such as adding properties to them, we do run the risk of incompatibility with app models that iterate over objects/properties/attributes and directly perform validation without going through `Validator` to do so. We will also need to think this through, do some discovery around where knowledge of these attributes has been baked in, and understand what that impact would be.

Just my 2 cents but the thing that really prevents me from liking attribute approach is that there are no types to solidify this validation. After validation it's just a plain string/int/whatever. No context attached.

I believe it's better to invest in roles or other kind of cheap flexible types and their support in mappers. Maybe some kind of IValidatable<TValue, TValidator> ?

Other thing is full fledged contracts.

I wouldn't personally want to see BCL introduce more of these as they are now and push people in a wrong (in my opinion) direction.

@jeffhandley Why is a block list an anti-pattern? Do they cause inherent problems? "Everything but X" can be substantially more concise than explicitly enumerating all values so it seems generally useful.

Regarding TimeSpanAttribute, I didn't realize this kind of thing was possible with the Range attribute. In our source base, we have a few uses of the overloads that accept an integer millisecond count, and a few uses of the Exclusive feature (so we can say "any timespan > 0"). We could easily convert the millisecond case to use the string form of the constructor. For the Exclusive case, if you expand Range attribute to support exclusive mode, then we'd be all set there.

> Why is a block list an anti-pattern? Do they cause inherent problems? "Everything but X" can be substantially more concise than explicitly enumerating all values so it seems generally useful.

Block Lists often connote that there's a finite list of possible values and some of those values are not permitted because they violate a business rule or can lead to unexpected behavior. In many contexts, this can lead to a false sense of security/safety, while a different value/permutation can just as easily lead to that unexpected state. With a finite list of possible values, an Allow List ensures only the known good states are permitted in the system, ensuring expected behavior. In any security-sensitive context, block lists are incredibly dangerous for this reason.

For a hypothetical scenario in a different context, we can imagine service configurations. A block list could be used to forbid a configuration of "development", "dev", "staging", etc. into a Production environment. But what would really be intended is to have an allow list of "production" or "prod" such that a configuration of "develop" or "local" would not be identified as valid.

This is clearly very context sensitive though, and there are certainly valid domain-specific block list scenarios. Allow lists should be used when feasible, and for those reasonable, domain-specific block list scenarios, I would recommend a domain-specific validator attribute. Such an approach encapsulates the business logic within the attribute by containing the allow-list/block-list approach and values within the validator without propagating the approach and values out to every reference site.

@geeknoid I see your point, but I disagree.

To flip your argument around, imagine I have a feature that must never be used in production, but can be used anywhere else since it's for diagnostics. Applying a black list that says "anything goes except production" is a perfectly reasonable thing to do.

I worry that "anything goes except production" is even more dangerous than the scenario I listed out. If an environment was named "prod" instead of "production," then that could lead to diagnostics being turned on in production when not intended. Instead, an allow-list of environments within which diagnostics are allowed to be captured is much less likely to have a false-positive.
A new use case came up lately which is a white list. A specification of the explicit set of values allowed. Kinda like Range, but for discrete values. I'd love to see an attribute for that too.
@geeknoid would it be possible to include an API shape for that attribute in the original post. Just a rough sketch or link to an equivalent implementation would suffice.

`[Range(typeof(TimeSpan), "<min-timespan-string>", "<max-timespan-string>")]`

This works. However it is arguably uglier to use and its internal implementation is playing [a guessing game](https://source.dot.net/#System.ComponentModel.Annotations/System/ComponentModel/DataAnnotations/RangeAttribute.cs,167) of how to compare a `TimeSpan`. Tailored implementation can instead use the type directly and thus be more efficient.

Note that C# now supports [generic attributes](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/csharp/language-reference/proposals/csharp-11.0/generic-attributes), so a generic Range attribute could be constrained to accept IComparable and simply accept two instances.

@roji Except [attribute parameters only support a limited set of types and `TimeSpan` is not among them](https://sharplab.io/#v2:C4LgbgpgTglgZgTwD4AEBMBGAsAKFwbQEEAKAEwjgEMBXAG2AEoBdXdAAkLZA+GFgCNqwCLgDeuNpLYoAzB2IAVGAFsIAZQAOlAHZtgAZwZtRAX1xm8OfAHEAPEtWadAPjIUa9ZqzRs7C51w8fDCCwmISUrK+imwAHkam5kA).
Thanks @svick, I missed that restriction..

@geeknoid regarding the proposed `LengthAttribute`, shouldn't there be provision for the `MinimumLength` value also being optional? It is conceivable that somebody might want to require string lengths up to a given upper bound.
@eiriktsarpalis Yes, it would be conceivable to make minimum length optional. It just makes the constructors a tad more complicated.

A few comments:

* Can LengthAttribute support strings, arrays, and collections?

* How about the dedicated attribute for timespans? We use this a lot.

Thanks.

Will the Range attribute gain support for comparing arbitrary objects with IComparable so that it can compare time spans? How will it handle exclusive boundary conditions? "Anything more than 0" or "anything less than 10ms"?

> Will the Range attribute gain support for comparing arbitrary objects with IComparable so that it can compare time spans?

I believe it [does so already](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/77402#issuecomment-1349797903), although it does force users to express upper and lower bounds as strings for types that do not support literals. 

> How will it handle exclusive boundary conditions? "Anything more than 0" or "anything less than 10ms"?

If I'm understanding the question correctly, in the `IComparer` contract `x.CompareTo(y) <= 0` means `x <= y` and `x.CompareTo(y) < 0` means `x < y`. We can use that to enforce exclusivity depending on user configuration.

> 1. `Base64StringAttribute`
>    
>    * This would generally not be used for end-user UI scenarios, which makes it a bit unusual for DataAnnotations validator attributes
>    * We should discuss if we want to be open to scenarios where the models being validated are not UI-oriented
>    * There are plenty of other non-validation attributes in the namespace that are not UI-oriented
>    * If we do open the door for those though, where will we draw the line? If we have a Base64String validator, would that inviteWellFormedJsonString or WellFormedXmlString?

IMO the validation namespace is already generic / non-UI specific and I wouldn't see any need to impose a scope limit to just UI now. I use data validation attributes in all kinds of applications (console, web desktop and mobile, services). Data validation isn't UI specific.

> If we do open the door for those though, where will we draw the line? If we have a Base64String validator, would that inviteWellFormedJsonString or WellFormedXmlString?

IMO I wouldn't restrict the scope of potential validators purely based on what they logically do, but rather judge them on a case by case basis on their effort required to introduce and their level of impact to customers.

I'm marking the issue as `api-needs-work` since it has come up that there is desired to use the new functionality in .NET framework. Even though `DataAnnotations` are not part of `netstandard2.0`, they do have implementations in .NET framework so adding new members to existing types becomes challenging from a type forwarding perspective.
The sooner the better, but if we can't get to it for another week, that's ok.
Then I suggest we push it to next week so we don’t have to time box too much. My gut feel is that interop stuff will take a while, probably even two rounds of reviews.

Per @eiriktsarpalis this is the better place to make the case for replacing the use of the word "Exclusive" with "Included" for the range attributes, thus finally addressing the remaining problems with the original and current names. This isnt a knock against whomever chose those names because naming can be hard. Also English is an overly complicated language with lots of odd and inconsistent rules.   I am aware that c# is not English but our programs that do use English words should be borrowing ones with unambiguous meanings.


"Exclusive" is more commonly used to describe "something special, limited, or unique that anyone can get, but only from one source". Like "exclusive content" that a media company might generate, or an "exclusive story" that a journalist may write about (but that everyone can access). In this attribute you intend to mean some strict mathematical usage that is something like the opposite of that. By using "Exclusive" there is an easy point of confusion with an everyday English word.

If you dont feel there is any confusion with using any form of "Exclude" then you must recognize that it qualifies as a negative name, which does not follow long standing [convention](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/names-of-type-members) for booleans.  The new names actually go farther away from those conventions than the previous choices due to the placement of the "be" word.  

The intellisense argument is not logical and just satisfying someone's need to have things arranged the way they like them (I've been guilty of this in the past too). Switching the order of the "be" word to the middle makes it harder to select the correct property in intellisense, and putting four properties all starting with the same letter and being close in spelling means more keystrokes are required to select the property that I want to use when its not the first choice in the list. Instead of having two `I`'s and two `M`'s with one down arrow extra each at ~10 keystrokes, its now four `M`'s and ~14 keystrokes

I'm not going to be comfortable with using this attribute with its current naming scheme. I will just avoid using it (and require any usage of it in PR's that I have to approve to follow suit) because I know these names will be problematic for someone else later and create bugs.


Copied and summarized from a few posts already made 
https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/8134#issuecomment-1483911888
https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/8134#issuecomment-1512371283
https://github.com/dotnet/core/issues/8134#issuecomment-1537519763

> "Exclusive" is more commonly used to describe "something special, limited, or unique that anyone can get, but only from one source". Like "exclusive content" that a media company might generate, or an "exclusive story" that a journalist may write about (but that everyone can access). In this attribute you intend to mean some strict mathematical usage that is something like the opposite of that. By using "Exclusive" there is an easy point of confusion with an everyday English word.

The terms "exclusive" and "inclusive" are fairly standard when it comes to upper bounds and ranges. A quick web search on "exclusive range" should illuminate this. The reason why we went with "exclusive" over "inclusive" is that inclusive ranges are the default for `RangeAttribute`.

> The terms "exclusive" and "inclusive" are fairly standard when it comes to upper bounds and ranges

@eiriktsarpalis - Keep in mind that the person saying this is someone who has studied mathematics extensively (at some very prestigious universities) and for whom the notions of Inclusive/Exclusive are probably something understood as naturally as breathing. There's nothing wrong with that perspective, but it is rather unique and rare. Many in our profession have a degree in a different field of study (Phd Biology, MS Communication, etc), some have taken no college classes, some didn't complete high school.  We read "exclusive" and have to cognate for a few moments or stop and look it up.  If the word were "Included", that impediment to reading the code would not happen.

> A quick web search on "exclusive range" should illuminate this.

There are also 71 Million web search results for "exclusive range is confusing" XD  

Do most English speakers recognize the word "bounds" as in "Leaps and bounds" or "out of bounds"? I dont know, but it could be either. Getting rid of the word "bounds" from the name was a good move. "Exclusive" needs the same treatment.  Even changing it to "Excluded" would be better than "Exclusive".  EDIT: "Inclusive" isn't really any better than "Exclusive" . 

When there is a more common, more easily understood, or less ambiguous naming alterative, that should be what is used.

While you're right that mathematical jargon should not necessarily always transfer to programming APIs, my point is that this is fairly established terminology from the perspective of programming APIs. A quick web search should highlight this, there are examples of this in [C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.range?view=net-8.0), [Rust](https://web.mit.edu/rust-lang_v1.25/arch/amd64_ubuntu1404/share/doc/rust/html/std/ops/struct.Range.html), [Scala](https://www.scala-lang.org/api/2.13.x/scala/collection/immutable/Range$.html), [Ruby](https://rubyapi.org/3.2/o/range), [Java](https://guava.dev/releases/19.0/api/docs/com/google/common/collect/Range.html) and the list goes on.

> there are examples of this in [C#](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.range?view=net-8.0), [Rust](https://web.mit.edu/rust-lang_v1.25/arch/amd64_ubuntu1404/share/doc/rust/html/std/ops/struct.Range.html), [Scala](https://www.scala-lang.org/api/2.13.x/scala/collection/immutable/Range$.html), [Ruby](https://rubyapi.org/3.2/o/range), [Java](https://guava.dev/releases/19.0/api/docs/com/google/common/collect/Range.html) and the list goes on.

I read that and these phrases were ringing in my head...
> "everyone else is doing it"  

> "Nobody get fired for choosing IBM"  

if you do the same thing as everyone else, it's not improving or adding value. That's like repeating a pattern from existing code for the reason of consistency when you know a better pattern. You have a chance to set a better precedent, don't waste it

> when you know a better pattern.

I don't actually. We're talking about terminology here, so what is "better" here is really a matter of established convention. I've shown beyond reasonable doubt that inclusive/exclusive is the established terminology, both in the context of mathematics and in the context of programming.

> That's _like_

Keyword there is "like" - I'm giving a similar situation where you would likely choose the opposite.  "Better" in this case has nothing to do with convention, and everything to do with readability and less defects.  

If you dont want to use a more common, more easily understood, and less ambiguous naming alterative, thats up to you.

review_comments: why we don't do that in the constructor?

Good question. This appears to be standard practice in DataAnnotations attributes, see for example `MinLengthAttribute`:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/71034dd2fbbd2304fac5c24d3a9f764a3c65f781/src/libraries/System.ComponentModel.Annotations/src/System/ComponentModel/DataAnnotations/MinLengthAttribute.cs#L47-L59

I'm guessing it's because the original authors would rather avoid throwing exceptions at attribute construction time and force these errors at validation time.
We throw in the constructors in other cases, I guess. It looks weird to me to throw during the validation and not during the construction. I'll leave it to you to decide the best here.

None of the other validation attributes appear to be throwing on the constructor. I'd probably have the constructor throw as well if I was writing this from scratch, but it's pretty clear that delayed argument validation was intentional (presumably because some validator component depends on validation attributes being queryable even if they are invalid? Maybe @jeffhandley knows)

I'd be inclined to preserve that invariant in the new attributes for the moment.

@eiriktsarpalis It was certainly a rule in .NET Framework that the attributes needed to be constructable without throwing. As I remember it, this was for design-time scenarios in Visual Studio. I don't know if it is relevant anymore.

I concur with the comments above that we tried to avoid throwing in constructors so that metadata models and design-time scenarios could construct the attributes without error. I also don't know to what degree that tenet is still relevant, but I'd be anxious about deviating from it without knowing how it would/could affect other systems.

Example scenario that is no longer applicable: Waaaaayyy back in the day, one of the scenarios was the build-time codegen we did for WCF RIA Services where we'd read the live code from an ASP.NET project and generate source files into a linked Silverlight project.

>return true; [](http://example.com/codeflow?start=16&length=12)

Is this the expected behavior?

Yes. Compare with other string validators like `PhoneAttribute`:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/71034dd2fbbd2304fac5c24d3a9f764a3c65f781/src/libraries/System.ComponentModel.Annotations/src/System/ComponentModel/DataAnnotations/PhoneAttribute.cs#L25-L28

The idea is that `null` validation is the responsibility of `RequiredAttribute` which has already been run, so other attributes will not try to intercept nulls.

I wanted to echo @eiriktsarpalis's comment here. It's important for every validator to indicate a Valid state for null values so that they can be used on _optional_ properties. As was said, it's exclusively the job of `RequiredAttribute` to ensure values are present.
What about the case of e.g. minimum==1, maximum==2 and both are exclusive?
I considered it but ultimately didn't want to introduce validation that is specific to integers. Other types might also define discrete orders but we wouldn't be able to validate these.
So we're just trying to flag some mistakes a dev might make and we're ok with false negatives, is that right?

Correct, it would be impossible to detect every empty range for arbitrary comparers. I could try special casing a check for integers but it seems unlikely people would use exclusive bounds on integer types.
